passages.title: Course project and ownership
passages.excerpt: I built my first neuromechanical model
passages.after: I built my first neuromechanical model in AnimatLab, a graphical program in which a neural circuit can activate muscles and receive sensory signals from the moving body \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}. For the course project, Morrow and I connected the circuit of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019} to the sagittal-plane biped of \citet{li_bipedal_2017} and adjusted neural currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters by hand. The circuit supplied a common rhythm to both legs, and opposing muscles pulled on each limb. I added a passive toe joint. The legs cycled in suspension, but the model tipped when released toward the ground (Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture}). Hunt and I reported the suspended model in a poster for the NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting \citep{bolenTorqueValuesArtificialKnee2021June15-17}. Each parameter change required another slow run, making a systematic search impractical.
passages.judgment: Model construction is Bolen’s. The two students coupled and tuned the system for a course. The poster has its own attribution.

passages.title: Tools and validation in the overview
passages.excerpt: I developed the tools in this chapter
passages.after: I developed the tools in this chapter to couple neural controllers to Gait2392, a human musculoskeletal model, and to mechanical models based on the computer-aided design (CAD) of our bipedal robot. Slow simulation and hand tuning in an earlier course project with Connor Morrow made it difficult to repeat the same experiment after changing the controller or the mechanical model. A scripted version of the walker in the MuJoCo physics engine made automatic tuning possible. The subsequent experiments use the human model, a robot counterpart with relocated muscle paths, and a model built from the lab robot's own geometry. I built a graphical editor to construct neural circuits for these experiments. A simulated knee reflex tests whether a sensory signal passes through a motor neuron and muscle to produce joint motion. The final experiments use scripts to tune controllers, test whether the feet alternate under load, and measure how much a faster neural calculation saves over a complete trial.
passages.judgment: The reader encounters a practical limit, the models and editor, a sensory-to-motion check, and automated experiments in order. Action verbs identify the author’s contributions.

passages.title: Why common recordings matter
passages.after: The fall could arise from a late extensor command, insufficient muscle force, or a small moment arm. Moving a muscle attachment can change its moment arm and, in a circuit that senses muscle length, the stretch signal returned to the controller. Distinguishing these explanations requires recording the neural command, muscle force, joint motion, and sensory feedback on the same clock while changing one part of the model at a time.
passages.judgment: A fall alone leaves three explanations open. Simultaneous recordings can show where the two trials first differ.

passages.title: Force at matched poses
passages.excerpt: To check whether the converted muscles
passages.judgment: OpenSim and MuJoCo receive the same pose and activation. The comparison reports a large single-pose difference for rectus femoris and a large mean bias for the short head.

passages.title: Reason to edit a connectome graphically
passages.after: AnimatLab provides a drawing surface for wiring neurons and synapses. In the SNS-Toolbox workflow, the researcher specifies those connections in Python and can render a diagram of the resulting network \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010,nourse_sns_2023}. A diagram helps locate a pathway. An editable diagram also lets the researcher change the connection where it is drawn. I built a graphical circuit editor and a library of Simulink blocks to make selected pathways in a connectome, the map of connections among neurons, accessible in this way. A nonspiking neuron continuously transmits changes in membrane voltage through its synapses over their operating range. A spiking neuron signals by emitting a discrete spike when its voltage reaches threshold. Scripts remain useful for generating repeated connections and testing many parameter settings. Table~\ref{tab:sns_capability} identifies the tools used for each task.
passages.judgment: The paragraph distinguishes drawing, rendering Python-defined networks, and editing the connection being inspected. The neighboring paragraph gives the scale and an extensor example.

passages.title: Library or example builders
passages.after: In the graphical editor, a researcher can place nonspiking neurons, draw synapses between them, inspect a synapse's strength and reversal potential, and save the circuit. The Build action generates a Simulink circuit from that saved description. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_signal_contracts} gives the editor command and build script. The knee and arm examples use separate builders to add their actuator, sensory, and mechanical blocks.
passages.judgment: The editor generates a Simulink circuit. The knee and arm builders supply their separate actuator, sensory, and mechanical blocks.

passages.title: Knee coupling test
passages.after: In the simulated knee, a brief pulse to the extensor Ia sensory input recruited the extensor motor neuron, increased extensor force, and extended the knee. The stimulated knee reached \ang{1.09} more extension than the control \qty{111}{\milli\second} after pulse onset (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_reflex_current}). The aligned traces show the order of the response. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_knee_transient} gives the wiring, initial conditions, and recovery test.
passages.judgment: The electrical stimulus leads through extensor recruitment and force to a measured change in knee angle.

passages.title: Arm coupling test
passages.after: As the simulated cup filled, the arm descended and stretched the biceps. With feedback enabled, the circuit recruited the biceps, which increased the force of its pneumatic actuator. The arm sagged \ang{2.00} with nonspiking feedback and \ang{7.85} with feedback disabled at the end of the same load ramp (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_beverage_current}). Together, the knee and arm examples verify that these blocks transmit sensory input to muscle force and return the mechanical response to the circuit. Appendix~\ref{sec:spiking_results} gives the matched spiking comparison.
passages.judgment: A changing external load closes the loop in the other direction. The feedback-on and feedback-off trial use the same loading ramp.

passages.title: Journal source for training
passages.after: I adapted the four-stage training method of \citet{hunt_development_2017} to the human model. The first stage sets the intrinsic period to approximately twice the target locomotor period. The second tunes the circuit to synchronize with the sensory input. The third fits feedforward motor recruitment, and the fourth refines it with sensory feedback. The recruitment targets came from inverse mechanics applied to reference motion. Agreement with those targets measures how closely the circuit reproduces the estimated muscle activation.
passages.judgment: Bolen adapted the sequence. Hunt, Szczecinski, and Quinn published its four stages and the doubled target period.

passages.title: Suspended cycling
passages.after: With the same fitted weights, the Gait2392 model cycled both legs in each suspended trial (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_biw2l_air}). The period shortened from \qty{2.466}{\second} to \qty{1.300}{\second} in the second trial. Both sensory feedback and sustained neural drive changed between trials, so this comparison cannot attribute the shorter period to feedback alone. The feet carried no load. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_biw2l_air} gives the controller settings, support forces, and joint-angle measurements.
passages.judgment: A measured difference remains, alongside the simultaneous change in drive and feedback and the absence of foot loading.

passages.title: Neural timing
passages.excerpt: A knee that flexes too little
passages.after: A knee that flexes too little gives no direct indication of where the error arose. To check the neural command, I tested syn6, a controller that distributes muscle recruitment among six pattern-formation channels in each leg of the Gait2392 human model. In the original circuit, the fifth channel continued to excite its motor neurons during the part of the cycle when it should have been silent. Changing the connection strengths improved the fit to muscle recruitment while leaving that timing error in place. Recording the signal leaving the channel showed which part of the controller needed revision.
passages.judgment: A constantly active channel identifies a timing defect in the controller. Separate neural and kinematic recordings identify residual bursts and limited movement in the later suspended trial.

passages.title: Supported contact
passages.after: On supported level ground, the W2L experiment asked whether the feet still alternated when selected sensory pathways were removed. Drive, assistance, and the forward perturbation were held fixed. With the controller intact, the heels struck almost half a cycle apart, a pattern called antiphase coordination. Removing force feedback through the Ib pathways alone preserved that timing. Removing heel and toe contact, pooled extensor-force inputs, and their associated spinal connections together moved heel strikes outside the alternation criterion, even though the model continued forward (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_ablation_pair}). The force records exposed a loss of coordination that forward distance alone would have missed (Appendix~\ref{sec:app_w2l_perturbations}).
passages.judgment: Under the same assistance and drive, a combined pathway removal disrupted footfall phase while the body continued forward.

passages.title: Existing tools
passages.excerpt: I developed the SNS-Simscape block library and graphical editor
passages.after: I developed the SNS-Simscape block library and graphical editor so that a researcher can draw a nonspiking circuit, inspect an individual connection, and generate a Simulink model from the saved circuit. The actuator and sensory blocks link muscle recruitment to force and joint motion in the single-joint demonstrations. For experiments with MuJoCo mechanics, the adapted interface sends actuator commands to a prepared model and returns joint and actuator measurements. The mechanical preparation tools make the Gait2392 human model, its rerouted robot counterpart, and a model assembled from the lab robot's CAD available for controller experiments.
passages.judgment: The block library, editor, adapted interface, and model preparation are identified with their present operations.

passages.title: Existing controlled comparisons
passages.after: The calibration and recording scripts make comparisons repeatable. A future researcher can load a saved circuit, change one sensory pathway, and repeat the trial with the body, drive, and support held fixed. The recordings show how that change affects neural activity, muscle force, joint motion, and foot contact. A change in muscle routing can be tested with the controller settings held fixed. The sparse neural implementation shortens repeated trials on the tested Gait2392 controller (Table~\ref{tab:sns_runtime}). These capabilities allow researchers to use human mechanics as a reference and simulate how a change in the controller or the robot's design affects coordination.
passages.judgment: A researcher can change a circuit or route, hold the other part fixed, and observe coordination, with a scoped timing result.

passages.title: Next sensory experiment
passages.excerpt: Future researchers can test whether particular
passages.after: Future researchers can test whether particular sensory inputs contribute to the extra bursts in the third pattern-formation channel during movement. The suspended six-synergy trial provides a record of the extra bursts and the joint motion at their onset. Replaying the same recorded motion while changing one sensory pathway at a time can distinguish the effect of that pathway from the accompanying change in knee angle. The layer-specific stimuli already tested in a reduced circuit can then be applied to the six-synergy controller under load. Stimulating the rhythm generator, a pattern-formation channel, or a motor neuron in separate trials can distinguish a reset of the rhythm from a missing motor burst with preserved phase (Section~\ref{sec:app_layer_stimulus}). Published responses provide a reference for those interventions \citep{selionov_tonic_2009,rybak_modelling_2006,markin_afferent_2010,shevtsova_modeling_2016}.
passages.judgment: Apply the existing layer-specific protocol to the six-synergy controller under load; distinguish replay timing from the variability of the moving body.

passages.title: Next mechanical experiment
passages.after: The force comparison in Appendix~\ref{sec:muscle-models-compare} identifies two muscles for a separate mechanical test. Future researchers can prescribe the same motion and activation history to rigid- and compliant-tendon models, then vary activation with the tendon model fixed. On the robot model, a measured pressure history can drive a characterized BPA route. Repeating a controller or contact experiment with that force law tests whether the force available at the measured length changes coordination.
passages.judgment: Vary tendon mechanics or activation separately, then test a characterized BPA force law with recorded pressure.

passages.title: Future embedded comparison
passages.excerpt: shows how future researchers can test
passages.after: Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline} shows how future researchers can test the embedded interface before connecting the biped's valves. A real-time leg simulation can supply measurements to the physical controller and receive its actuator commands. Recorded signals can first exercise the sensory encoder, the command interface, and the watchdog that detects stale commands. After the compiled neural controller is connected to the hardware inputs and outputs, replaying the same perturbation through the software and embedded controllers would expose sampling delays, missed updates, or scaling errors. Figure~\ref{fig:simulation_workflow} identifies the existing simulation interfaces, and Appendix~\ref{sec:app_embedded_interfaces} describes the hardware components.
passages.judgment: A real-time reference and replayed perturbation can test the hardware interface before valve actuation.

passages.title: Advisor’s Introduction ending
passages.excerpt: The sensory pathways documented in the database
passages.after: The sensory pathways documented in the database suggest how the nervous system uses feedback from the legs to coordinate movement. To simulate what those pathways contribute, it is possible to combine a neural circuit model with the mechanical model of the body it controls. The circuit activates muscles, their forces move the joints, and the resulting changes in muscle stretch and load feed back to the circuit and shape its next commands. The robot’s artificial muscles differ from human muscles in how much force they produce and where they pull on the skeleton. A circuit that coordinates the legs of the human model will therefore produce a different movement in the robot model, and that movement will change the sensory feedback the circuit receives. To measure the effect of the mechanics, I wanted to repeat the same experiment on both models with the controller held fixed. I also wanted to test changes to the controller while keeping the mechanical model fixed. Our first neuromechanical model ran slowly, and we tuned its controller by hand, making a series of these comparisons impractical. I therefore developed tools to build circuits graphically, automate their tuning, and run those comparisons on a human musculoskeletal model and on models built from our robot's mechanical design (Chapter~\ref{ch:sns}). With human movement as a reference, the new system can simulate how changing a sensory connection or moving an artificial muscle attachment affects a mechanical model's coordination.
passages.judgment: The exact live paragraph connects mechanics and feedback to controlled comparisons, states what the system can simulate, and preserves Ben’s preposition.

passages.title: Two muscle discrepancies
passages.after: Eight muscles had force-agreement scores of 0.88--0.98 and mean forces within \qty{10}{\percent} of OpenSim. The rectus femoris mean ratio was 1.088, but the force estimates followed different patterns across poses ($r^2=0.384$). Its summed squared force error was about 2.15 times the mean-reference squared error. For biceps femoris short head, the shape correlation was higher ($r^2=0.868$), but the mean ratio of 1.846 indicates that the converted actuator produced about \qty{85}{\percent} more force on average. Its squared error was about 1.26 times the mean-reference error. Both scores compare errors in force magnitude at matched poses.
passages.judgment: The negative scores have an explicit constant-force reference. Separate variation and mean magnitude explain the two cases.

passages.title: Controller timing and mechanical outcome
passages.after: I changed how the channels started and stopped their bursts. The revised circuit met its timing targets with prescribed sensory inputs calculated from the reference movement. When the moving, suspended legs supplied their own feedback, a subsequent repair kept the second channel to one burst per cycle, but the third still produced three or four bursts. The trial completed with the knee-extension limit respected, but its rhythm missed the acceptance criteria. The phase-averaged knee curves spanned \ang{19} on the left and \ang{34} on the right, compared with about \qtyrange{70}{72}{\degree} in the walking references (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_syn6_overlay}). Individual cycles varied, so the average curves conceal some of the knee motion. The extra bursts identify a remaining timing error in the controller. Neither foot supported weight in this trial. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_pf_timing} gives the timing criteria and trial conditions.
passages.judgment: The timing target was met with prescribed inputs. In a completed suspended run, the third channel produced extra bursts and the rhythm failed its acceptance criteria. The seven-cycle mean knee excursions are observed in the same trial.
